characters: Ato: an 11-year-old boy in a school uniform, with paint on his fingers.
Ofosua: his classmate, 11, in a school uniform with a red ribbon in her hair.
Mr Bortey: their teacher, in a white shirt and tie, holding a paintbrush and a small flag.
Theodosia Okoh: a woman artist and teacher in a plain dress, seated at a desk drawing the flag (story picture).

narrationPlan.voice: Bright, proud teacher’s voice for Mr Bortey; eager young voices for Ato and Ofosua
narrationPlan.pace: Proud and clear, brighter at the colours (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Bright highlife brass and drums building to a proud, open finish (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The Ghana flag was adopted on 6 March 1957. This story uses published accounts and an invented teacher and pupils.
The meanings of the colours and star are widely taught; sources and speakers sometimes give slightly different readings, and the story says so.
The story names a real designer, Theodosia Okoh, as a person of achievement and does not describe her private life.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check against named sources: adopted 6 March 1957; designed by Theodosia Okoh, an artist and teacher; the colours; the black star and its link to the Black Star Line; the 1960s change and the restoration (sources give 1962 to 1966 and 1966; confirm).
The claim that Ghana was the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence from European colonial rule is widely stated but disputed at the edges; confirm the wording or soften it.
Check that the portrayal of Kwame Nkrumah is fair and brief, and ask a Ghanaian historian to review.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about the flag as a symbol and about the real person who designed it. It teaches the meaning of national symbols, how widely told meanings can still vary, and how historians handle a change of dates.
learningGoals: Name the designer, colours and star of the Ghana flag and explain their meanings.
Explain why a flag is a symbol.
beforeReading: Ask: why does every country have a flag? What does yours say about the people?
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners to match each colour to its meaning.
afterReading: Design a flag for your class and explain each colour and shape.
Write a short paragraph about Theodosia Okoh as a person who made something that lasts.
discussion: Why might two people give different meanings to the same colour?
What does a flag need so that everyone can recognise it?
reflection: What would your class flag say about you?

mathsExtension.task: From 6 March 1957 to 2026 is how many years?
The flag has three stripes. If each is 20 cm tall, how tall is the flag?

support: Give learners a flag outline and labels to place.
stretch: Compare the Ghana flag with the flags of two other African countries and discuss shared colours.

culturalNotes: The Ghana flag was adopted on 6 March 1957. This story uses published accounts and an invented teacher and pupils.
The meanings of the colours and star are widely taught; sources and speakers sometimes give slightly different readings, and the story says so.
The story names a real designer, Theodosia Okoh, as a person of achievement and does not describe her private life.
localiseThis: Link to national days and school assemblies; follow school rules on handling the flag.

whatWeKnow: Theodosia Okoh designed the flag adopted on 6 March 1957.
The flag was later changed for a few years and then restored in the 1960s.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The exact years of the change, which sources give differently.
Whether every detail of the colour meanings is official or has grown in popular teaching.

factCheck.claim: The flag was adopted on 6 March 1957; Theodosia Okoh, an artist and teacher, designed it; red, gold and green stripes with a black star; the star is linked to Marcus Garvey’s Black Star Line and to the national football team’s nickname; the flag was changed in the 1960s and the original reinstated in 1966.
factCheck.explanation: From Wikipedia’s Flag of Ghana article, which itself carries a tone notice and has weak support for the colour meanings, and whose dates for the 1960s change are inconsistent.
factCheck.reference: Wikipedia, “Flag of Ghana”. Check also the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board and national archives.

factCheck.claim: Ghana gained independence from Britain on 6 March 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah; the flag was designed by Theodosia Salome Okoh; red stands for those who died for independence, gold for mineral wealth, green for the land and the black star for the people and African emancipation.
factCheck.explanation: From South African History Online, which also calls Ghana the first to gain independence from European colonialism.
factCheck.reference: South African History Online, “Gold Coast (Ghana) gains independence”.

pronunciation.guidance: "KWAH-meh". English speakers often say "KWAH-mee"; confirm the final vowel.
reviewerNotes: Confirm final vowel (meh vs mee) and the "kw" onset.
